title: A contact path for a restaurant group
metaTitle: A contact path for a restaurant group
excerpt: Tell a guest what happens after they reach out, how soon, and what to have ready. Booking a table and asking about a private room are different paths. Ten fields lose the night.
alt: A glass-walled office corridor with a sofa, a floor lamp, and black pendant lights, a hallway that only works if a visitor can tell where they are supposed to go next.
caption: A corridor with a place to sit. A guest still needs to know which door is theirs. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Should guests use a contact form to book a table?
faqs.answer: No. A table for tonight should go through the booking link for that restaurant, with the venue already chosen. A contact form is for the paths the widget cannot hold, such as a private room or a buyout. Mixing them in one ten-field form loses both the table and the event.

faqs.question: What should a private dining note ask?
faqs.answer: Date, number of people, which room, and a way to reply. Say what happens next and how soon, in a window you keep. Ask for the menu preferences after you know the date is possible. A long form that starts with marketing questions will lose the inquiry.

faqs.question: What if someone just wants the menu?
faqs.answer: Send them to the menu for that restaurant, as text on the phone, without a form. The contact page should not be a gate in front of prices or dishes. Hours and address belong in the open too, so a guest does not have to write to you to learn you are closed.

markdown:
A restaurant group contact page should tell a guest deciding where to go tonight what happens after they reach out, how soon, and what to have ready. The action they usually need is simpler: see the menu or book a table. A form with ten fields is a way to lose them.

Most nights, this page should be a signpost, not a questionnaire. Point to the menu. Point to the booking link for the right room. Keep a short path for the requests a widget cannot take.

## Two paths, labeled

Split the page in the first screen. Book a table. Ask about a private room. Those are different products. A two-top at eight is a widget. A room for eighteen is a person. If you blend them, the widget will reject the party and the inbox will fill with ordinary bookings the widget should have handled.

Write the table path as links, one per restaurant, already aimed at that venue. Say the hours beside the link so a guest does not request a Monday you are dark. [Google's helpful content guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks whether a reader leaves able to act. Acting tonight is opening the menu or holding a table. The contact page fails when it makes them write an email to do either.

The private path can be a short form. Say what it is for, in the heading. "Private dining and buyouts." Not "Contact us," which means everything and then means nothing at 6 p.m.

If you also take press, suppliers, or job applications, give them one line and a different address. Do not put them above the guest. The guest is the reason the page exists. Everyone else can scroll.

## What happens after they reach out

For a table, say what the widget's confirmation means. A held booking. A request the restaurant still has to accept. A deposit. Guests should not discover the meaning at the last step if you can say it in a sentence beside the button. If the widget's own screen already says it clearly, do not contradict it on your page.

For a private note, say the sequence. You read it. You reply with a yes, a no, or one missing fact. If it is a yes, you send the menu and the minimum. If it is a no, you say so, and you point at the public rooms if a normal table would work. That sequence is the product of this path.

Name who replies. "The events lead writes back" is better than "the team." A guest planning a dinner for their boss wants a person. If the chef does not answer these notes, do not imply that they do.

Say what you will not do from a cold email. You will not hold a Saturday on a vague note with no date. You will not design a custom menu before the headcount exists. The boundary saves the inbox and sets a serious guest at ease.

## How soon, and what to have ready

Publish a reply window you keep on a Friday. A day is often honest for private dining. Same evening is honest only if someone is actually watching the inbox during service. Do not borrow a speed from a hotel brand. A missed promise costs the event.

Tell them what to include so the reply can be useful. Date, time, number of people, which restaurant. A note on speeches or a cake if that changes the room you offer. That is enough for the first message. Allergies and seating plans can wait until the date is real.

Do not ask how they heard of you, their company size, or a file upload before you know the date. Those fields feel responsible in a CRM demo. On a phone they are how the inquiry dies. You can ask the useful extra on the reply.

Put the list on the page so they can gather it before they type. A guest in a taxi should know that the date and the headcount are the whole job.

[The W3C's WCAG overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) is the quality bar for the form itself. Labels visible, not placeholders that vanish. Errors in words. A button that says what it does. Fields that work with a phone keyboard. The principles are perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. A form that fails them fails the guest who was ready.

## Ten fields lose the table

The long form is the failure mode. It asks for a vision, a budget dropdown you invented, a preferred cuisine inside your own group, and a newsletter opt-in before the note can send. Each field was added after one awkward call. Together they tax the guest who already chose you.

Cut the table path out of the form entirely. Cut the private form back to date, headcount, room, name, and email. Five lines. You will still have a conversation. You will have more of them.

Watch for other losses. A captcha that fails. A required phone number for a guest who only uses email. A map as the only way to pick a restaurant. Two restaurants with the same button. Fix those before you add a new question.

Read the last twenty private inquiries. Circle the facts that changed your reply. Those are the fields. The rest were curiosity. Curiosity can live in the reply you send, where a human can skip what does not matter.

## The menu still does the real work

This page should not become a second homepage. The room and the dish live elsewhere. Here, repeat the paths and the promise, then stop. Link to each menu in text. A guest who landed on contact from a search for your name may still need the dishes more than a form.

Keep a visible email for people who will not use a form, and say which notes belong there. Private dining to one address. Press to another, if you must split. One address that a person reads is better than a grid of departments nobody checks during service.

Confirm a send on the page. "We have the date and the headcount. We will reply within one working day." Repeat the window. Do not dump them into a void with a coupon.

If the paths are tangled and you want them drawn before a rebuild, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). Bring the widget, the form, and a week of messages that should never have been emails. Hanabi designs and builds the page so the table stays a link and the private note stays short. The copy has to match what the floor will do, because the floor keeps the promise.

### A check on a Friday

Send yourself both paths from a phone. Book a test table and cancel it properly. Send a private note with only the five facts and see whether a human can answer without writing back for the date. If you cannot, the form did not ask for the one thing you need, or it asked for so much that you skipped your own test.

Read the auto-reply. If it says the inquiry is important and does not repeat the window, rewrite it. If it does not say which restaurant the note was about, add that. The guest should not have to remind you which door they chose.

Do this when the events person is actually on the inbox, not only when the site launches. A perfect form into a mailbox nobody opens on Friday is a closed restaurant with good typography. The path includes the habit. Write the habit next to the window you published, in the staff note, not only on the website.

## Where the paths must appear

The contact page is the long version. The paths themselves belong on the homepage and on each restaurant. A guest who has chosen a room should see Menu and Book on that page, aimed at that room, without a detour through a general inbox. Private dining can be a text link under the public booking, not a second hero.

Use one reusable block at the end of a restaurant page. The hours. The address. The two buttons. A line that private parties use the short note. Keep the full explanation here, so you do not maintain five different promises. If a restaurant page ends with "follow us" and no table, replace that ask. A social link can live in the footer. It is not the night.

Say which room a note started from if they write from that page. A hidden field with the restaurant name is enough. You should not ask them to retype a door they can see. In the inbox, you should know whether the note is Holt Street or the wine bar before you reply with the wrong minimum.

Read the block on a phone during service hours. The buttons have to clear the browser chrome. The hours have to be true that day. Send one test booking and one test private note. Both should land where a person looks, with the window you published. If the events inbox is unattended on Saturdays, do not promise Saturday replies. Change the sentence. The path includes the roster, not only the fields.

## What the rest of the site should stop doing

A clear path still fails if the homepage performs taste and hides the room. A logo animation will feed this page with confused guests and will fail to feed the widget with ready ones. The contact page cannot rescue a site that never showed a dish.

The cut list is [what not to put on the site for a restaurant group](/blog/what-not-to-put-on-the-site-for-a-restaurant-group). Read it with the form open. Anything that delays the room, the menu, or the table is a candidate to leave off.
